# Interplay of Crystal Field Splitting and Hund Coupling in a Two-Orbital Model

## Overview

This study investigates the intricate interplay between crystal field splitting and Hund coupling within a two-orbital model that is particularly relevant to physical systems containing two electrons or two holes in the e_g shell. Understanding how these two fundamental interactions cooperate and compete is essential for describing the electronic properties of a broad class of correlated materials, where the local atomic environment and electronic correlations jointly determine the ground state.

## Methodology

To address this problem, the researchers employ single-site dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), a powerful framework for capturing local quantum fluctuations in strongly correlated electron systems. A key methodological advance in this work is the development of a new impurity solver that is capable of reliably accessing regimes of strong coupling and low temperatures. This capability is crucial, as these regimes are often difficult to reach with conventional numerical techniques, yet they are precisely where the most interesting correlation-driven phenomena tend to emerge.

## Results

Using this approach, the authors systematically compute orbital fillings and phase boundaries as functions of the key parameters governing the model: the Coulomb repulsion, the exchange (Hund) coupling, and the crystal field splitting. Mapping out these quantities allows for a comprehensive characterization of the phase diagram and reveals how the system responds to variations in each of these competing energy scales.

The calculations uncover several notable features. Most strikingly, the Hund coupling can drive the system into a novel Mott insulating phase, distinguished by a vanishing orbital susceptibility. This behavior highlights the pivotal role that Hund coupling plays not only in setting the scale of electronic correlations but also in stabilizing distinct insulating states.

Furthermore, when the system is tuned away from half-filling, the crystal field splitting is found to induce an orbital-selective Mott state. In this regime, one orbital becomes localized while the other remains itinerant, demonstrating that the crystal field can selectively drive a subset of orbitals into a Mott-localized condition.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these findings clarify how crystal field splitting and Hund coupling jointly shape the phase behavior of two-orbital systems. The identification of a novel Hund-driven Mott phase with vanishing orbital susceptibility, alongside the emergence of an orbital-selective Mott state induced by crystal field splitting away from half-filling, provides valuable insight into the rich physics of multi-orbital correlated materials.

# Interplay of Crystal Field Splitting and Hund Coupling in Two-Orbital e_g Systems

## Motivation and Model

Multi-orbital correlated electron systems host a rich variety of physical phenomena that emerge from the competition between several energy scales. Among these, the crystal field splitting and the Hund coupling play a particularly important role in shaping the electronic structure of transition-metal compounds. In this work, we investigate the interplay of these two effects within a two-orbital model designed to capture the essential physics of e_g-shell systems. Such systems are of considerable interest because the e_g doublet is generically subject to lifting of its degeneracy by the crystalline environment, while the on-site electron-electron interactions—including the Hubbard repulsion and the Hund exchange—strongly influence the correlated behavior of the electrons.

## Methodology

To treat the local correlations non-perturbatively, we employ single-site dynamical mean field theory (DMFT), which maps the lattice problem onto a self-consistently determined quantum impurity model. The reliability of our conclusions rests on the use of an impurity solver capable of reaching the regime of strong couplings and low temperatures, where conventional perturbative or high-temperature approaches break down. This allows us to compute the orbital fillings and to map out the phase boundaries of the model across a broad range of interaction strengths and crystal field splittings.

## Results

Our central findings concern the emergence of distinct correlated insulating states driven by the two competing mechanisms.

First, we find that the Hund coupling can drive the system into a novel Mott insulating phase characterized by a vanishing orbital susceptibility. In this state, the strong Hund exchange locks the orbital degrees of freedom in such a way that the system becomes insensitive to perturbations that would otherwise redistribute charge between the orbitals. This behavior distinguishes the phase from conventional Mott insulators and highlights the active role of Hund physics in stabilizing unconventional correlated states.

Second, when the system is tuned away from half-filling, we observe that the crystal field splitting can induce an orbital-selective Mott state. In this regime, one orbital undergoes localization while the other remains metallic, reflecting the differing effective fillings and correlation strengths of the two orbitals. The crystal field splitting thus provides a control parameter that selectively drives one orbital into the Mott insulating regime, producing a coexistence of localized and itinerant electronic character.

## Significance

Taken together, these results illustrate how the combination of crystal field splitting and Hund coupling generates a phase diagram richer than that of the single-orbital Hubbard model. The identification of a Hund-driven Mott phase with vanishing orbital susceptibility, alongside the crystal-field-induced orbital-selective Mott state away from half-filling, deepens our understanding of the correlated physics of e_g-shell materials and offers guidance for interpreting experiments on real transition-metal compounds where these energy scales compete.

# Hund's Rules and the Coulomb Interaction

## Introduction

In atomic and condensed matter physics, understanding how electrons arrange themselves within partially filled shells is a fundamental problem. **Hund's rules**, formulated by the German physicist Friedrich Hund, provide a set of guidelines for determining the ground state electronic configuration of atoms. At the heart of these rules lies the **Coulomb interaction**—the electrostatic force between charged particles.

## The Coulomb Interaction

The Coulomb interaction describes the repulsive force between two electrons, which carry the same negative charge. Because electrons repel one another, their spatial arrangement is not arbitrary; nature seeks configurations that minimize the total electrostatic energy of the system. This repulsion is expressed mathematically as:

$$V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{e^2}{r}$$

where *r* is the distance between the two electrons. The Coulomb interaction, combined with the quantum mechanical requirement of antisymmetry for fermions, gives rise to subtle effects that shape the electronic structure of matter.

## Hund's Rules

Hund's rules emerge as a direct consequence of the interplay between the Coulomb repulsion and the Pauli exclusion principle. The rules can be summarized as follows:

1. **Maximize total spin (S):** Electrons preferentially occupy orbitals with parallel spins. Because electrons with the same spin must occupy different spatial orbitals (due to the Pauli principle), they tend to stay farther apart, reducing the Coulomb repulsion energy.

2. **Maximize total orbital angular momentum (L):** For a given spin configuration, the state with the largest allowed value of L is favored, again because this arrangement minimizes electron repulsion.

3. **Determine total angular momentum (J):** For shells that are less than half-filled, J = |L − S|, while for shells more than half-filled, J = L + S. This rule arises from the spin-orbit coupling.

## The Physical Significance

The genius of Hund's insight was recognizing that the seemingly abstract rules of quantum mechanics have a concrete physical origin in the Coulomb interaction. When electrons align their spins, the antisymmetry of the total wavefunction forces their spatial parts to be antisymmetric as well, creating an "exchange hole" that keeps electrons apart and lowers the electrostatic energy.

## Applications

Hund's rules and the underlying Coulomb physics are essential for understanding:

- **Magnetism** in transition metals and rare-earth elements
- **Optical spectra** of atoms and ions
- **The properties of strongly correlated materials**, where Coulomb interactions dominate

## Conclusion

The connection between Hund's rules and the Coulomb interaction illustrates a beautiful principle in physics: complex emergent behavior can arise from fundamental interactions. By understanding how electrons minimize their mutual repulsion within the constraints of quantum mechanics, we gain deep insight into the structure of atoms and the diverse magnetic and electronic properties of materials.

**Interplay of Crystal Field Splitting and Hund's Coupling in a Two-Orbital Hubbard Model: A Dynamical Mean-Field Study**

**Abstract**

We investigate the competition between crystal field splitting and Hund's exchange coupling in a two-orbital Hubbard model using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) with a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo impurity solver. Focusing on the half-filled and quarter-filled regimes, we map out the phase diagram as a function of the interaction strength $U$, the Hund's coupling $J$, and the crystal field splitting $\Delta$. We find that these two energy scales act antagonistically: while a finite crystal field favors orbital polarization and can drive a band-insulating or orbitally-selective state, the Hund's coupling suppresses orbital differentiation by penalizing double occupancy within a single orbital and enforcing high-spin configurations. As a result, an increasing $J$ shifts the metal–insulator boundary and stabilizes a correlated metallic phase over an extended parameter range, exhibiting the hallmark "Hund's metal" behavior characterized by strong quasiparticle mass renormalization and a separation of spin and orbital screening scales. We further show that the crystal field can trigger an orbital-selective Mott transition, in which one orbital localizes while the other remains itinerant, and we analyze how this transition is modified by $J$. Our results are quantified through the evolution of the local spectral functions, orbital occupations, quasiparticle weights, and local spin and orbital susceptibilities. These findings clarify the microscopic mechanisms governing electronic correlations in multi-orbital materials such as transition-metal oxides and provide guidance for interpreting spectroscopic and transport signatures in systems where crystal field and Hund physics coexist.

# Abstract

## Interplay between Hund's Coupling and Crystal Field Splitting in $e_g$-Orbital Systems: A Dynamical Mean-Field Theory Study

We investigate the correlated electronic structure of two-orbital $e_g$ systems, focusing on the competition and cooperation between Hund's exchange coupling ($J$) and crystal field splitting ($\Delta$) using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) combined with a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo impurity solver. While the physics of Hund's metals has been extensively explored in $t_{2g}$-dominated compounds, the role of Hund's coupling in $e_g$ manifolds—where orbital degeneracy is more readily lifted by lattice distortions—remains comparatively underexplored. Here we systematically map the phase diagram as a function of interaction strength $U$, Hund's coupling $J$, crystal field splitting $\Delta$, and filling.

Our calculations reveal that Hund's coupling and crystal field splitting act as antagonistic forces governing orbital polarization: $J$ tends to enforce a high-spin, orbitally balanced configuration by penalizing double occupancy of individual orbitals, whereas $\Delta$ drives orbital differentiation and, ultimately, orbital selectivity. At half filling ($n=2$), we identify a spin-freezing crossover and a Hund's-assisted Mott transition whose critical $U_c$ is strongly renormalized by $\Delta$. Away from half filling, we observe an orbital-selective Mott phase in which the lower $e_g$ orbital localizes while the upper orbital retains itinerant character, stabilized by the synergy of correlations and finite crystal field.

We further demonstrate that Hund's coupling suppresses orbital polarization induced by $\Delta$, effectively screening the crystal field and rigidifying the local moment. This "Hund's screening" of crystal field splitting has direct consequences for the effective mass enhancement, quasiparticle coherence scale, and local spin susceptibility. Our results provide a unified framework for interpreting the correlated properties of $e_g$-based transition-metal oxides, including nickelates, manganites, and layered ruthenates under epitaxial strain, and offer concrete predictions for how lattice engineering of the crystal field can be used to tune correlation strength and magnetic behavior.

We present a comprehensive single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) study of the phase diagram of a two-orbital Hubbard model, systematically mapping the phase boundaries as functions of the local Coulomb repulsion $U$, Hund's exchange coupling $J$, and crystal field splitting $\Delta$. Employing a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo impurity solver, we resolve the interplay between these three energy scales across a range of band fillings, with particular emphasis on integer occupancies where correlation-driven metal-insulator transitions occur. Our calculations reveal that the boundary separating the metallic and Mott-insulating phases shifts markedly with $J$, reflecting the competition between the Hund's-coupling-enhanced local moment formation and the reduction of the effective critical interaction at half filling. The resulting three-dimensional phase diagram, spanned by $U$, $J$, and $\Delta$, provides a unified framework for understanding the rich correlated behavior of multiorbital systems and offers guidance for interpreting the electronic properties of transition-metal oxides and related compounds where these parameters can be tuned by chemistry, strain, or pressure.

# Abstract

Hund's coupling has emerged as a central organizing principle in the physics of multiorbital correlated systems, giving rise to phenomena ranging from "Hund's metals" to orbital-selective Mott transitions. While much attention has focused on partially filled t₂g-shell materials, the role of Hund coupling in eₒ-shell systems remains comparatively unexplored. The transition into this state is accompanied by a marked reduction of the critical interaction strength and a characteristic reorganization of the local spin and orbital correlations, which we track through the temperature and coupling dependence of the relevant susceptibilities and spectral functions. Our results demonstrate that Hund coupling can act not merely to modulate metallicity but to select a qualitatively distinct insulating ground state with quenched orbital degrees of freedom. These findings provide a unified framework for understanding the correlated physics of eₒ-shell compounds and suggest experimental signatures—most notably an anomalously suppressed orbital response—that can distinguish this Hund-driven Mott phase in candidate materials.
